questions.question: A circle graph is cut into 4 equal parts. One part is shaded and labelled 25%. The whole circle stands for 80 students in a Grade 7 class. How many students does the shaded part stand for?
questions.explain: A percent on a circle graph is a share of the whole, not a head count: 25% of 80 is 80 ÷ 4 = 20 students. The common trap is copying the label and saying 25 students — the 25 is 'out of every 100', and this class only has 80.

questions.question: A circle graph is cut into 10 equal parts. Three of the parts are shaded together and labelled 30%. The whole circle stands for 200 books in a classroom library. How many books does the shaded piece stand for?
questions.explain: The shaded piece is 30% of the whole, so it stands for 0.30 × 200 = 60 books. The trap is reading 30% as 30 books; the percent tells you what share of the 200 the piece is, not how many books there are.

questions.question: A circle graph is cut into 5 equal parts. Two parts are shaded and labelled 40%. The whole circle stands for 45 minutes of recess. How long is the shaded part?
questions.explain: The whole circle is 45 minutes, so 40% of it is 0.40 × 45 = 18 minutes. Saying 40 minutes treats the percent as if it were the amount itself, but 40% has to be taken of the 45 minutes the whole circle stands for.

questions.question: A circle graph is cut into 5 equal parts. One part is labelled 20%, and the whole circle stands for 60 juice boxes sold at a school fair. Which sentence about that one part is correct?
options: The slice stands for 20 juice boxes
The slice stands for 1 juice box
The slice stands for 48 juice boxes
The slice stands for 12 juice boxes
questions.explain: A slice labelled 20% means one fifth of the whole, so it stands for 0.20 × 60 = 12 juice boxes. The usual mistake is thinking the label 20% names the quantity itself; a percent only becomes a quantity after you take it of the whole.

questions.question: A circle graph shows how 250 students at a Surrey middle school get to school. The section for walking is 36%. How many students walk?
questions.explain: Take the percent of the whole survey: 0.36 × 250 = 90 students. The trap is answering 36, which would only be right if exactly 100 students had been surveyed.

questions.question: Nadia tracked the $400 she earned last summer on a circle graph. The section for snacks is 15%. How much money does that section stand for?
questions.explain: The section is 15% of the $400 whole, so 0.15 × 400 = $60. Reading the label as $15 is the common slip — the percent describes the size of the share, and the dollars come from taking that share of $400.

questions.question: A circle graph shows the 60 cans collected in a food drive. The soup section is 45%. Which calculation tells you the number of soup cans?
options: Read 45 straight off the graph: 45 cans
questions.explain: To turn a percent on a circle graph into a quantity you multiply the percent by the whole: 0.45 × 60 = 27 cans. Reading 45 straight off the graph treats a share as a count, which is only ever true when the whole happens to be 100.

questions.question: A circle graph shows the pets owned by 80 students. The cat section is 25%. How many of the students do NOT own a cat?
questions.explain: Cats are 0.25 × 80 = 20 students, so the rest is 80 − 20 = 60 students; you could also take 75% of 80 directly. The trap is writing 75 or 25 straight from the percents — those are shares out of 100, not students out of 80.

questions.question: A circle graph shows the favourite winter activity of 300 people surveyed at a Kelowna rec centre. Swimming is 24% and skating is 30%. How many more people chose skating than swimming?
questions.explain: Change each percent into people first: skating is 0.30 × 300 = 90 and swimming is 0.24 × 300 = 72, so the difference is 18 people. Subtracting the percents to get 6 gives a difference in share, not a number of people.

questions.question: Maya made a circle graph of the favourite fruit of 40 students in her class. The apple section is 35%, and she wrote underneath: '35 students chose apple.' What should she fix?
options: Nothing is wrong — the number on a slice tells you how many people chose it, so 35 is right
35% means 35 out of every 100, so the apple section stands for 14 of the 40 students
She should have written that 65 students chose apple, because 100 − 35 = 65 is the rest
She should have divided 40 by 35, giving about 1 student, since percents are shared out
questions.explain: A percent is a share out of 100, so it must be taken of the actual whole: 0.35 × 40 = 14 students. Only 40 students were surveyed, so 35 students choosing apple is impossible once you notice the percent is not a count.

questions.question: A circle graph shows how 500 students at a Vancouver school travelled to school this year, with 20% taking the bus. Next year the school will have 600 students, and the principal expects the same percents. How many students would take the bus next year?
questions.explain: The percent stays the same but the whole changes, so use the new whole: 0.20 × 600 = 120 students. Answering 100 uses this year's 500 students, and answering 20 treats the percent itself as the number of riders.

questions.question: A school bake sale raised $600. A circle graph shows cookies 40%, muffins 35%, and bread the rest. How much more money did cookies raise than bread?
questions.explain: Bread is 100 − 40 − 35 = 25%, so cookies raised 0.40 × 600 = $240 and bread raised 0.25 × 600 = $150, a difference of $90. Subtracting 40% − 25% to get $15, or calling the 25% section $25, turns a share into dollars without ever using the $600 whole.
